lessons.title: What is Organic Fertilizer? Differences from Compost
lessons.body:
Compost is decomposed organic matter that improves soil structure and feeds soil life, but it is not a concentrated fertilizer. Organic fertilizer, on the other hand, is a material that provides specific plant nutrientsâmainly nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K)âin higher concentrations. While compost typically has an N-P-K ratio of about 1-1-1 or less, organic fertilizers like bone meal (approx. 3-15-0) or blood meal (12-0-0) are much more potent. In Africa, common organic fertilizers include animal manures (chicken manure: 3-2-2), compost tea, bone meal, blood meal, rock phosphate (0-20-0), and wood ash (0-1-7).

Compost is made by piling carbon-rich materials (dry leaves, straw) and nitrogen-rich materials (kitchen scraps, manure) in layers, keeping it moist, and turning it regularly. It takes 4-8 weeks to mature. Organic fertilizer, however, is often a processed or concentrated product. For example, to make bone meal, you cook bones, dry them, and grind them into powder. To make blood meal, you collect blood from slaughterhouses, dry it, and grind it. These processes require more effort but yield a product that can be applied in small quantities to correct specific deficiencies.

Using compost alone may not supply enough nutrients for heavy-feeding crops like maize or tomatoes. That's where organic fertilizers come in. You can use them as a top-dress or mix them into the soil at planting. For instance, applying 200g of chicken manure per maize plant can boost yields, while compost is usually applied at 2-4 tons per hectare. Organic fertilizers are also faster-acting than compost, though still slower than synthetic fertilizers.

In summary, compost builds soil health; organic fertilizers feed plants. A smart African farmer uses both: compost to improve the soil and organic fertilizers to meet specific crop needs. Start by mastering compost, then expand into making and using organic fertilizers from local materials.

lessons.title: Making Liquid Fertilizer (Compost Tea) from Manure
lessons.body:
Compost tea is a liquid organic fertilizer made by steeping manure or compost in water. It is quick to make, easy to apply, and gives plants a fast nutrient boost. You can make it from fresh or dried chicken, cow, goat, or rabbit manure. The basic recipe: fill a sack (burlap or porous nylon) with 10 kg of manure, tie it, and suspend it in a 200-liter drum of water. Let it steep for 3-7 days, stirring daily. The water will turn dark brownâthat's your compost tea. For a stronger brew, add 1 kg of sugar or molasses to feed beneficial microbes. Keep the drum in the shade to avoid evaporation.

After steeping, remove the sack. The liquid is now ready to use. Dilute it with water at a ratio of 1:5 (one part tea to five parts water) for young plants, or 1:2 for mature crops. Apply it as a foliar spray using a knapsack sprayer, or pour it around the base of plants. For foliar feeding, strain the tea through a cloth to avoid clogging the sprayer. Apply early morning or late afternoon to prevent leaf burn. You can use compost tea every 2 weeks during the growing season.

Safety is important: always use manure from healthy animals, and wear gloves when handling. If you use fresh manure, the tea may contain harmful bacteria like E. coli. To reduce risk, let the tea brew for at least 5 daysâbeneficial microbes will outcompete pathogens. Alternatively, use aged manure. Never apply compost tea to leafy greens close to harvest; wait at least 2 weeks after application before eating them raw.

The leftover manure in the sack can be added to your compost pile. The drum can be reused many times. This method is cheap and effective: a 200-liter drum of tea can fertilize a quarter-acre of vegetables. Many farmers in Kenya and Nigeria use this technique to boost yields without buying expensive synthetic fertilizers. Try it on a small plot first and observe the results.

lessons.title: Preparing Bone Meal and Blood Meal at Home
lessons.body:
Bone meal and blood meal are two powerful organic fertilizers you can make at home from slaughterhouse waste. Bone meal is rich in phosphorus (about 15-20%) and calcium, making it perfect for root development and flowering. Blood meal is high in nitrogen (about 12%), ideal for leafy growth. Both are slow-release and safe for all crops. To make bone meal: collect clean animal bones from a butcher. Boil them for 1-2 hours to remove meat, fat, and pathogens. Then dry them in the sun for 3-5 days until brittle. Break them into small pieces with a hammer, then grind them into a fine powder using a mortar and pestle or a grain mill. Store the powder in a dry container. For blood meal: collect fresh blood from a slaughterhouse (cattle, goat, or pig). Let it clot, then cut into small chunks. Spread on a tarpaulin and dry in the sun for 3-4 days, turning daily until completely dry and crumbly. Grind into powder using a mortar or mill. Store in an airtight container away from moisture.

Application rates: Bone meal is best mixed into the soil at planting. Use 1-2 handfuls (about 100-200g) per planting hole for tomatoes, peppers, or root crops. For blood meal, apply 1 handful (about 50g) per plant as a side-dress, or mix 1 kg per 10 square meters before planting leafy greens like spinach or kale. Both can be blended with compost or wood ash. Do not overapply blood mealâtoo much nitrogen can burn plants or cause excessive leaf growth with few fruits.

Safety: Wear a dust mask when grinding to avoid inhaling particles. Wash hands and tools thoroughly. If you cannot grind bones finely, you can break them into small pieces and add them to compost; they will break down slowly. Blood meal can attract dogs or rodents, so store it in a closed container. In many African markets, you can sell excess bone meal or blood meal to other farmers. A 1-kg bag of bone meal can fetch $2-5, while blood meal sells for $1-3. This is a good income stream if you have access to slaughterhouse waste.

lessons.title: Using Rock Phosphate and Limestone Locally
lessons.body:
Rock phosphate and limestone are mined minerals that can be used as organic fertilizers if they are finely ground. Rock phosphate provides phosphorus (20-30% P2O5) and calcium, but it is slow-releaseâit needs acidic soil to dissolve. Limestone provides calcium and magnesium and raises soil pH. In Africa, rock phosphate is mined in countries like Morocco, Algeria, and South Africa, but you can also find local deposits. Limestone is more common. To use them, you must grind them into a fine powder. A hammer mill or ball mill is ideal, but you can also use a strong mortar and pestle. The finer the powder, the faster it works.

Application: Rock phosphate is best applied to acidic soils (pH below 6.5) and mixed into the root zone. Use 200-500g per planting hole for perennial crops like bananas or fruit trees, or broadcast 1-2 tons per hectare for field crops. It works slowly, so apply it 2-3 months before planting. For vegetables, mix 100g per square meter into the soil. Limestone is used to correct soil acidity. If your soil is too acidic (pH below 5.5), apply 1-2 tons per hectare of ground limestone. For a small garden, use 1-2 kg per 10 square meters. Mix it into the top 15 cm of soil. Do not apply limestone and rock phosphate together with manure in the same holeâthey can react and reduce availability.

Testing your soil: You can buy a simple pH test kit from an agro-vet shop. If pH is below 6, add limestone. If you need phosphorus, rock phosphate is a good choice. Both minerals are safe to handle, but wear a dust mask when grinding to avoid inhaling dust. Store in a dry place. In some areas, you can buy already ground rock phosphate from agricultural suppliers. Check with local farmer cooperatives. Using local minerals reduces dependence on imported fertilizers and builds soil health over time. Start with a small trial plot and compare with your usual practice.

lessons.title: Mixing Custom Fertilizer Blends for Vegetables
lessons.body:
Different vegetables need different nutrient ratios. Leafy greens like kale, spinach, and cabbage need more nitrogen. Root crops like carrots and onions need more phosphorus and potassium. Fruiting crops like tomatoes and peppers need a balance of all three, with extra phosphorus for flowering and potassium for fruit development. You can make custom blends using the organic fertilizers you have: compost, blood meal, bone meal, wood ash, and rock phosphate. Here are three simple recipes. For leafy greens: mix 4 parts compost, 1 part blood meal, and 1 part wood ash. This gives a nitrogen boost. Apply 2 handfuls per plant every 3 weeks. For root crops: mix 4 parts compost, 2 parts bone meal, and 1 part wood ash. Apply at planting and again 4 weeks later. For fruiting crops: mix 4 parts compost, 1 part blood meal, 2 parts bone meal, and 1 part wood ash. Apply at planting and again when flowers appear.

To mix, use a clean bucket or wheelbarrow. Measure by volume (e.g., a tin cup). Wear a dust mask and gloves. Mix thoroughly until uniform. Store in a dry sack or container. Use within 3 months. You can also add a handful of rock phosphate for long-term phosphorus. For a 10-liter bucket, use 6 liters compost, 1 liter blood meal, 2 liters bone meal, and 1 liter wood ash. This makes about 10 kg of blend. Apply 200-300g per plant for tomatoes, or 100g per plant for beans.

Test on a small area first. Observe plant growth: if leaves are yellow, add more blood meal; if fruits are small, add more bone meal or wood ash. Keep notes. You can also sell these blends in small bags to other farmers. Label clearly with the crop it suits. In Kenya, some farmers sell custom blends for $1-2 per kg. This adds value to your organic fertilizer production. Always use mature compost to avoid burning plants. Adjust recipes based on your soil and crop response.

lessons.title: Storing and Packaging Organic Fertilizer for Sale
lessons.body:
Proper storage and packaging are key to selling organic fertilizer. Moisture, sunlight, and air can reduce nutrient content and cause mold. Store your fertilizer in a cool, dry, dark place. Use airtight containers: plastic drums with lids, heavy-duty poly sacks, or sealed buckets. For long-term storage, keep in a dry room with low humidity. If you make bone meal or blood meal, store in sealed containers with a desiccant (like dry rice) to absorb moisture. Compost tea should be used within 2 days; it cannot be stored. Dry fertilizers like rock phosphate and limestone can last for years if kept dry.

Packaging for sale: Use clear, strong poly bags or woven sacks. For small-scale sales, pack in 1-kg, 5-kg, and 10-kg bags. Label each bag with: product name (e.g., 'Bone Meal'), N-P-K analysis (if known), net weight, your farm name, and contact. Include instructions: 'Apply 100g per plant' or 'Mix into soil before planting.' For liquid fertilizers, use plastic bottles with tight caps. Label with dilution instructions. You can also offer custom blends for specific crops, e.g., 'Tomato Booster'. Use a simple logo or sticker to build trust. In many African markets, customers prefer clear labeling and a consistent product.

Marketing: Sell at local farmers' markets, agro-vet shops, or through farmer groups. Price competitively: check what others charge. For example, a 1-kg bag of bone meal might sell for $2-3, while a 5-kg bag of compost might sell for $1-2. Offer bulk discounts. Keep records of sales and feedback. As demand grows, consider getting organic certification if you want to export. But for local sales, focus on quality and reliability. Always weigh accuratelyâshort-changing customers will ruin your reputation. With good packaging and storage, you can turn your organic fertilizer into a steady income stream.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Making Organic Fertilizer Beyond Compost

Compost is the foundation of any organic fertility programme, but compost alone rarely delivers the concentrated nutrients that high-value vegetables, fruit trees, or cash crops demand. For African agribusinesses â from a two-acre market garden near Kumasi to a 20-hectare horticultural operation supplying Nairobi supermarkets â the real margin lies in producing concentrated organic fertilizers: liquid teas, bone meal, blood meal, rock phosphate blends, and custom mixes tailored to specific crops and soils. This lesson is a hands-on reference for making, blending, storing, and selling those products.

Treat every product below as a business asset. Document your inputs, batch numbers, and nutrient analyses. Buyers â especially certified organic exporters and institutional caterers â will pay a premium for consistency and traceability.

1. What Is Organic Fertilizer? Differences from Compost

Compost is a bulk soil amendment â typically 0.5â2% N, 0.3â1% P, and 0.5â1.5% K on a dry basis â applied in tonnes per hectare to build organic matter and biology. Organic fertilizer, by contrast, is a concentrated nutrient product made from specific feedstocks (blood, bone, rock phosphate, manure teas) and applied in kilograms or litres per hectare. The distinction matters commercially: compost sells for US$20â60 per tonne; concentrated organic fertilizers can sell for US$200â1,500 per tonne because of nutrient density and handling convenience.

Sources: FAO (2015), Organic Farming: A Guide for Small-Scale Farmers; FiBL (2021), African Organic Agriculture Training Manual; NRC (2000), Nutrient Requirements of Beef Cattle (for blood/bone meal ranges).

2. Making Liquid Fertilizer (Compost Tea) from Manure

Compost tea is the fastest way to convert manure into a saleable liquid product. Two methods dominate in Africa:

  • Anaerobic steep (passive): Fill a 200-litre drum 1:3 manure to water, cover, and steep for 10â14 days. Stir daily. Cheap but odorous and lower in aerobic microbes.
  • Aerobic brew (actively aerated): Use a small air pump (aquarium type, 40â60 L/min) in a 200-litre drum with 1:5 manure-to-water ratio plus 200 g molasses. Brew 24â36 hours. Higher microbial diversity and less smell â the preferred product for commercial sale.

Filter through a 100-mesh screen or cloth. Dilute 1:5 with clean water before foliar application. For soil drench, use 1:3. Never apply undiluted tea to seedlings â it can burn leaves.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Pathogen and Odour Risk

Raw manure and blood can carry E. coli, Salmonella, and Listeria. Always wear gloves, boots, and a dust mask when handling dry manures and blood meal. Wash hands and tools with soap after handling. Do not apply manure tea to leafy greens within 90 days of harvest (120 days for root crops). Brew tea in a shaded, ventilated area away from homes and water sources. If you sell tea, label it "for ornamental and non-food crops" unless you have pathogen testing (e.g., E. coli < 1000 MPN/g). In Kenya, KEBS and the Organic Certification Body require pathogen testing for commercial organic inputs.

3. Preparing Bone Meal and Blood Meal at Home

Both products are by-products of abattoirs and are often wasted in African towns. With simple equipment you can turn them into high-value fertilizers.

Bone meal: Collect clean bones. Boil for 2â3 hours to remove fat and pathogens. Dry in sun or a solar dryer until brittle. Crush with a hammer mill or pestle to <2 mm. For faster phosphorus release, calcine (burn) at 500â700Â°C in a simple kiln â this converts hydroxyapatite to more plant-available forms. Sieve to 100 mesh for premium retail.

Blood meal: Collect fresh blood in a clean container. Dry in thin layers on a concrete slab or in a solar dryer (60â70Â°C) for 2â4 days until brittle. Mill to powder. Store in airtight bags. Blood meal is a fast-release nitrogen source (10â14% N) â excellent for leafy vegetables but easy to over-apply. Limit to 200â400 kg/ha for vegetables.

4. Using Rock Phosphate and Limestone Locally

Africa holds large deposits of rock phosphate (Morocco, Egypt, South Africa, Tanzania, Uganda) and limestone (Kenya, Zambia, Nigeria). Raw rock phosphate is slow-release â best for acidic soils and perennial crops. For annual vegetables, partially acidulate with local organic acids (e.g., compost leachate, vinegar) or blend with manure before application.

Limestone (calcium carbonate) and dolomite (calcium-magnesium carbonate) correct soil acidity. Apply based on soil test â typically 1â4 t/ha for acidic soils (pH < 5.5). In Kenya, the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) provides lime recommendations by county.

Sources: Adapted from FiBL (2021), African Organic Agriculture Training Manual, Module 5; and KALRO (2018), Fertilizer Use Recommendation for Kenya. Blends should be adjusted based on soil test results.

5. Mixing Custom Fertilizer Blends for Vegetables

Custom blending is where the highest margins are. Follow these steps:

  1. Soil test first. Use a local lab (e.g., KALRO, Crop Nutrition Laboratory Services in Nairobi) or a portable test kit. Know your pH, N, P, K, and organic matter.
  2. Set a target nutrient ratio for the crop (see Table 2).
  3. Weigh each ingredient on a calibrated scale. Accuracy is your brand.
  4. Mix in a concrete mixer or on a clean tarpaulin. Layer ingredients, then turn 3â4 times until uniform colour.
  5. Moisture check: Aim for 15â20% moisture. Too dry = dust; too wet = mould.
  6. Granulate (optional): Use a small disc or drum granulator with a molasses-water binder for a premium retail product.
  7. Sample and test each batch for N-P-K and pathogens before sale.

6. Storing and Packaging Organic Fertilizer for Sale

Organic fertilizers are hygroscopic and biologically active. Poor storage destroys value.

  • Moisture: Keep below 15% for dry products. Use moisture-proof liners (HDPE) inside woven polypropylene bags.
  • Temperature: Store below 30Â°C, out of direct sun. Heat kills microbes and volatilises nitrogen.
  • Liquid teas: Use within 24â48 hours of brewing, or refrigerate. For retail, stabilise with 1% molasses and sell within 7 days, or concentrate and bottle with preservatives (citric acid).
  • Packaging: 1 kg, 5 kg, 25 kg, and 50 kg bags. Label with product name, N-P-K, batch number, production date, expiry, and use instructions. Include a QR code linking to a simple usage guide â this builds trust with buyers.
  • Compliance: In Kenya, register with KEBS and the Organic Certification Body (e.g., KOAN). In Nigeria, NAFDAC registration is required for packaged fertilizers. In Uganda, MAAIF regulates.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Source feedstocks from at least two suppliers to avoid disruption (manure, bones, blood, rock).
  • â Test every batch for N-P-K and pathogens before sale â keep a logbook.
  • â Brew compost tea with aeration for 24â36 hours; never sell undiluted or unpreserved tea older than 48 hours.
  • â Dry blood and bone meal to <12% moisture; mill and sieve to consistent particle size.
  • â Blend custom mixes only after soil testing; label with exact N-P-K and crop recommendation.
  • â Store in a cool, dry, shaded warehouse on pallets â never on bare ground.
  • â Package in moisture-proof bags with batch number, date, and clear usage instructions.
  • â Register your product with the national regulator (KEBS, NAFDAC, MAAIF) before commercial sale.
  • â Train workers on hygiene and safety â gloves, masks, handwashing, and no eating in the production area.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Organic Farming: A Guide for Small-Scale Farmers (free PDF)
  • FiBL â African Organic Agriculture Training Manual (free download)
  • KALRO â Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (soil fertility & lime recommendations)
  • Organic Africa â Knowledge Hub for Organic Agriculture in Africa
  • IFOAM â Organics International (standards and certification guidance)

Prepared for Rise AFRICA Skills â Organic Fertilizer & Compost. Use this reference alongside your practical field sessions and local extension officer guidance.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between compost and organic fertilizer?
options: A) Compost is synthetic, organic fertilizer is natural.
B) Compost improves soil structure, while organic fertilizer provides concentrated nutrients.
C) Compost is faster-acting than organic fertilizer.
D) Organic fertilizer is only made from minerals.
quiz.explanation: Compost primarily builds soil health, while organic fertilizers supply specific nutrients in higher concentrations.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of an organic fertilizer with a high phosphorus content?
quiz.explanation: Bone meal is rich in phosphorus (about 15-20%), making it ideal for root and flower development.

quiz.q: What is the typical N-P-K ratio of compost?
quiz.explanation: Compost generally has a low and balanced nutrient content, often around 1-1-1 or less.

quiz.q: Which material is used to make blood meal?
quiz.explanation: Blood meal is made from dried and ground animal blood, providing high nitrogen.

quiz.q: How long should manure steep in water to make compost tea?
quiz.explanation: Steeping for 3-7 days allows nutrients and beneficial microbes to extract into the water.

quiz.q: What is the recommended dilution ratio for compost tea applied to young plants?
quiz.explanation: A 1:5 dilution (one part tea to five parts water) is safe for young plants to avoid burning.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid applying compost tea to leafy greens close to harvest?
options: A) It makes leaves taste bitter.
B) It can contain harmful bacteria like E. coli.
quiz.explanation: Manure-based tea can harbor pathogens; waiting at least 2 weeks reduces health risks.

quiz.q: What is the first step in making bone meal at home?
options: B) Boil bones to remove meat and fat.
C) Dry bones in the sun.
quiz.explanation: Boiling cleans the bones and removes pathogens before drying and grinding.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is blood meal primarily rich in?
quiz.explanation: Blood meal is high in nitrogen (about 12%), promoting leafy growth.

quiz.q: How should bone meal be applied for best results?
options: B) Mixed into the soil at planting
C) Dissolved in water and poured on leaves
quiz.explanation: Bone meal is slow-release and works best when mixed into the root zone at planting.

quiz.q: What is a safety precaution when grinding bones or blood?
options: B) Do it in a closed room.
D) Add water to reduce dust.
quiz.explanation: Inhaling dust from bone or blood meal can harm lungs, so a mask is essential.

quiz.q: Which mineral fertilizer is known for raising soil pH?
quiz.explanation: Limestone contains calcium carbonate, which neutralizes acidity and raises pH.

quiz.q: What is the ideal soil pH range for rock phosphate to be effective?
quiz.explanation: Rock phosphate dissolves better in acidic soils (pH below 6.5) to release phosphorus.

quiz.q: How finely should rock phosphate be ground for best results?
quiz.explanation: The finer the powder, the greater the surface area for nutrient release.

quiz.q: What is a common application rate for limestone in a small garden?
quiz.explanation: For small gardens, 1-2 kg per 10 square meters is typical to correct acidity.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid mixing limestone and rock phosphate together with manure in the same hole?
options: A) They can react and reduce nutrient availability.
quiz.explanation: Chemical reactions between these materials can lock up nutrients, making them less available to plants.

quiz.q: Which crop would benefit most from a fertilizer blend high in nitrogen?
quiz.explanation: Leafy greens like kale need more nitrogen for leaf growth.

quiz.q: In a custom blend for fruiting crops like tomatoes, which ingredient provides potassium?
quiz.explanation: Wood ash is a good source of potassium (about 7% K2O) for fruit development.

quiz.q: What is a recommended mixing ratio for a leafy green fertilizer blend?
options: A) 4 parts compost, 1 part blood meal, 1 part wood ash
B) 4 parts compost, 2 parts bone meal, 1 part wood ash
C) 4 parts compost, 1 part blood meal, 2 parts bone meal
D) 2 parts compost, 2 parts bone meal, 1 part wood ash
quiz.explanation: This blend provides extra nitrogen from blood meal for leafy growth.

quiz.q: How should custom fertilizer blends be stored?
options: B) In a dry, cool place
quiz.explanation: Moisture and heat degrade nutrients, so a dry, cool location is best.

quiz.q: What is a good practice when selling packaged organic fertilizer?
options: A) Label with N-P-K and instructions
quiz.explanation: Clear labeling builds trust and helps customers apply correctly.

quiz.q: Why should compost tea be used within 2 days?
options: A) It loses nutrients and can become anaerobic.
quiz.explanation: Without aeration, beneficial microbes die and pathogens may grow, so fresh use is best.

quiz.q: Which of these is a suitable container for storing dry organic fertilizer?
quiz.explanation: Airtight containers prevent moisture and pests from damaging the fertilizer.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of packaging organic fertilizer in small bags?
options: A) Easier for customers to buy and use
quiz.explanation: Smaller packages are more affordable and convenient for small-scale farmers.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a slow-release organic fertilizer?
quiz.explanation: Rock phosphate releases nutrients slowly over months or years.

quiz.q: What is the typical nitrogen content of blood meal?
quiz.explanation: Blood meal is high in nitrogen, usually around 12%.

quiz.q: How can you test if your soil needs limestone?
options: A) Use a pH test kit
quiz.explanation: A pH test kit indicates acidity; if pH is below 6, limestone may be needed.

quiz.q: What is a common source of bones for making bone meal?
quiz.explanation: Slaughterhouses provide clean animal bones that can be processed into bone meal.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is wood ash particularly rich in?
quiz.explanation: Wood ash contains about 7% potassium, useful for fruit and root development.

quiz.q: What is a recommended application rate for blood meal as a side-dress?
quiz.explanation: A small handful (about 50g) per plant provides a nitrogen boost without burning.

quiz.q: Why is it important to label homemade organic fertilizer with instructions?
options: A) To ensure correct application and avoid crop damage
B) To make it look professional
quiz.explanation: Proper instructions prevent over-application and help customers get good results.
